name: Lincoln Spear
description:
Lincoln Spear is the district where wealth learned to grow thorns. Old Lincoln Park was Chicago's jewel — the zoo, the conservatory, DePaul University's leafy campus, brownstones whose price tags required six figures just for the down payment. When the Corporate Reconstruction sorted Meridian into tiers, Lincoln Park's existing wealth made the transition almost seamlessly. The residents who could afford to stay became Tier 3 and 4. The residents who couldn't were encouraged to relocate with the kind of encouragement that involves changing the locks. The neighborhood didn't fall. It rose — and then it built walls to make sure nothing could pull it back down.

The Lincoln Park Zoo is still here, though what it contains has changed. The megafauna are gone — too expensive to maintain when the climate shifted and supply chains collapsed. In their place: bioengineered specimens from Meridian's pharmaceutical and genetics corporations, housed in the zoo as a combination of public relations showcase and living patent library. Visitors can observe animals that don't exist in nature — luminescent arctic foxes, miniature elephants the size of dogs, birds that sing corporate jingles encoded into their vocal patterns. The conservatory has been converted to a sealed-environment agricultural laboratory where Axiom-subsidiary Verdant Dynamics tests crop strains that may never feed anyone outside the upper tiers. The grounds are immaculate. The admission fee requires Tier 3 credentials. The message is clear: nature is a luxury good, and you're welcome to look but not to touch.

DePaul University survived the reconstruction by becoming something its Vincentian founders would not recognize: a corporate training academy. The campus is intact — the old brick buildings, the tree-lined paths, even the chapel — but the curriculum is Axiom-approved, the student body is Tier 3 and above, and the degrees conferred are effectively corporate certifications with academic window dressing. The faculty are compliant because compliance is a condition of employment, and the few who push back find their contracts terminated with the polite efficiency that Axiom applies to all its optimization projects. Students emerge fluent in corporate culture, competent in their specializations, and largely incapable of questioning the system that produced them. It's the most successful education program in Meridian, by every metric that matters to the people who define the metrics.

The Spear's border with the districts below is the sharpest class boundary in northern Meridian. The transition from North Branch Commons to Lincoln Spear happens across a single block — on one side, cooperative schools and parent patrols; on the other, manicured hedgerows and private security drones. The Spear's residents don't think about this boundary. They've been trained not to. The security systems, the credential checks, the cultural assumption that anyone from below who appears in the Spear must be there on a work permit — these things are invisible to the people they protect and obvious to everyone else. Kyle has been in the Spear exactly twice, both times on contract, both times pretending to be someone with better credentials. He doesn't like it here. It's too clean. Clean, in his experience, means someone else is doing the dirty work somewhere you can't see it.

sights: Manicured green spaces maintained by automated groundskeeping drones — unnervingly perfect lawns
The zoo's bioengineered exhibits visible through transparent enclosure walls — creatures that glow, shimmer, and shouldn't exist
DePaul's campus, eerily unchanged from a century ago — brick, ivy, bell tower — wrapped in invisible security mesh
Private security drones on silent patrol, their Axiom subsidiary branding tastefully minimized
Brownstone residences with original architectural details preserved by nano-restoration technology
The class boundary — visible from the Spear's southern edge, the abrupt transition from wealth to survival
sounds: Silence — real silence, the expensive kind that requires active noise cancellation systems embedded in the streetscape
Birdsong from the zoo's engineered specimens — musically perfect, algorithmically composed
DePaul's chapel bells on the hour — a recording now, but a faithful one
The whisper of private security drones overhead — barely audible, deliberately so
Conversation at a tasteful volume — the Spear's residents have been socialized to speak quietly
smells: Engineered floral scents from the park's atmospheric management system — lavender, jasmine, and something unnamed that promotes calm
Fresh-cut grass — the Spear is one of the few places in Meridian with enough real grass to cut
The conservatory's sealed-environment agriculture — botanical richness contained behind glass
Nothing offensive — the atmospheric management system filters the air. The Spear smells like a curated absence of smell.
atmosphere.feel: Anesthetized. Lincoln Spear is beautiful the way a display model is beautiful — everything in place, nothing out of order, every sensory input managed for maximum pleasantness. The discomfort isn't in what you experience but in what you don't: no visible poverty, no audible distress, no olfactory evidence that the city outside exists. The Spear feels like someone deleted the parts of reality that make wealthy people uncomfortable and replaced them with landscaping.

demographics: Approximately 15,000 residents, predominantly Tier 3 and Tier 4. Corporate middle management, licensed professionals, DePaul faculty and advanced students. Demographically homogeneous in a way that is statistically improbable and obviously engineered. The service workers who maintain the district commute in from the Commons and Lakeview Neon on daily work permits.
economy: Corporate-adjacent professional services, DePaul's tuition economy, zoo and conservatory tourism, and high-end residential real estate. The legal economy is clean. The service economy that supports it is not — Lincoln Spear's comfort requires an army of underpaid workers who go home to districts that look nothing like this.
power_structure: Axiom subsidiary governance through the Lincoln Spear Residents' Association, which is technically elected and practically controlled by corporate interests. DePaul's administration functions as a secondary power center. Private security answers to the Residents' Association, which answers to Axiom's regional management. Democracy as decorative element.
dangers: Getting caught without credentials — the Spear's security systems are thorough and the penalties for unauthorized presence are severe
Corporate surveillance — everything in the Spear is monitored, recorded, and analyzed
Social engineering traps — the Spear's professional class is a target-rich environment for con artists with good wardrobes
The security drones — non-lethal in theory, painful in practice, and autonomous enough to make mistakes
Complacency — the Spear's residents are so insulated that they make easy marks for anyone who penetrates the perimeter
opportunities: Corporate intelligence — the Spear's professional class has access to information that's valuable in the right markets
DePaul's library — one of the few intact pre-collapse academic archives in Meridian, accessible to students and staff
The zoo's bioengineered specimens — genetic material worth fortunes to the right buyer
Service worker infiltration — the daily work permit system creates a constant flow of lower-tier individuals through the Spear's interior
High-value contracts — the Spear's residents occasionally need problems solved that their security systems can't handle
story_hooks: A DePaul professor contacts Kyle through five layers of intermediaries — she's found something in the university archives that contradicts Axiom's official history of the Corporate Reconstruction, and she needs it extracted before the administration discovers what she's been reading

One of the zoo's bioengineered specimens escapes containment and makes it to the Commons — a creature worth millions in genetic patents, now hiding in a children's playground. The zoo wants it back quietly. Several other parties want it permanently.

A Lincoln Spear resident's child has gone missing — not kidnapped, but deliberately descended into the lower districts. The parent is offering a fortune for recovery. The child doesn't want to be recovered.
frequented_by: Corporate professionals living the Tier 3-4 lifestyle Axiom designed for them
DePaul students and faculty operating within the approved curriculum
Service workers commuting in on daily permits from lower-tier districts
Zoo and conservatory visitors with the credentials to afford admission
Private security personnel — human and drone — maintaining the curated normalcy
